case_study_insert.main_stem: Little Sprout Clothing Cooperative (LSP) is a cooperative in the childrenswear retail sector, based in Portland, Oregon, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2019 by Sophie and Dan Whitmore, it sells new and refurbished children's clothing through one shop and online, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. LSP plans to invest $350,000 in a pre-loved childrenswear e-commerce platform with a garment repair workshop, financed by a $220,000 bank loan and $130,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. LSP faces a skills gap, with only 6 of 28 staff trained in garment repair and refurbishment.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — September 2026: A survey of 500 parents found that 71% would buy pre-loved children's clothing online and 64% already resell items informally. The pre-loved childrenswear market grew 18.5% last year. Last year 9,600 of the 40,000 units LSP sold were refurbished garments. Among parents aged 25-40, 57% cited sustainability as their main reason to buy resale, and the average saving versus new was $14 per garment. Current repair turnaround averages 5 days.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Little Sprout Clothing Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 5.5%, increasing borrowing costs for small businesses on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% to $13.60 per hour from April 2027, raising wage costs for the cooperative. (3) The online resale market grew 18.5% last year and is forecast to expand a further 15.0% in 2027, while consumer spending on childrenswear rose 5.1%.

questions.question_text: LSP plans to fund the pre-loved platform with retained profit and a bank loan. Explain two advantages for LSP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $130,000 of retained profit avoids additional interest and repayment obligations on top of the $220,000 bank loan, protecting LSP's modest liquidity — cash and cash equivalents stood at just $50,000 in 2025. Every dollar not paid as interest can fund repair workshop equipment and keep refurbished garments affordable for parents, which is central to LSP's cooperative mission.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and decision-making entirely with the worker-members, consistent with cooperative principles. No external lender can attach conditions on wages, staffing or the social mission; members retain full democratic control of the platform, and LSP avoids over-reliance on debt that could threaten the $210,000 fixed-cost base if resale demand is slower than the 15.0% forecast growth, or if borrowing costs rise again.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to LSP's finance decision, cooperative structure and platform investment.

questions.question_text: LSP is launching its pre-loved childrenswear platform and repair workshop. Consider hosting local community repair events, partnering with parenting influencers on social media or distributing printed flyers through libraries and nurseries. Which should LSP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local community repair events: Free or low-cost 'bring your children's clothes' mending and styling mornings in the shop let parents touch refurbishment quality first-hand, meet the Whitmores, swap resale tips with the 64% who already resell informally, and sign up to the platform on the spot. Word-of-mouth in parent networks is powerful, the cash cost is minimal against $210,000 fixed costs, and it expresses the cooperative's community ethos better than any advert. Its limit is reach beyond the Portland catchment.

Parenting influencer partnerships: Local influencers could present pre-loved childrenswear styling to thousands of followers quickly and drive traffic to the platform with affiliate codes. However, fees are paid regardless of results, endorsements can feel commercial for a cooperative brand, attribution for in-person shop visits is weak, and a poor influencer match could alienate the 57% of sustainability-minded buyers LSP most wants.

Printed flyers in libraries and nurseries: Flyers are cheap, tactile and reach parents with young children exactly where clothing decisions are made. But print response rates are typically very low, design and distribution must be repeated for every nursery, and there is no way to measure which venue delivered customers — poor value when every dollar matters to a 28-person cooperative.

Recommendation: LSP should choose local community repair events. They convert the cooperative's core differentiator — genuine garment repair skill and trust — into platform sign-ups at near-zero cash cost, and they build durable word-of-mouth in a city where 71% of parents say they would buy pre-loved online. Flyers are rejected as unmeasurable and low-yield, influencer marketing is rejected as too expensive for a launch budget and at odds with LSP's character, with a modest influencer test layered in later once the platform proves itself.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to LSP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of LSP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of LSP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why flyers and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: LSP faces a skills gap, with only 6 of 28 staff trained in garment repair. Explain two benefits for LSP of using democratic leadership to close this skills gap.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the workforce design the training plan — the 6 skilled repairers can volunteer, colleagues can state which skills they want, and members agree the workshop timetable together. Training people choose is training they complete, and closing the gap lifts LSP's capacity to handle 9,600 refurbished garments a year and the growing online orders.

Point 2: Involvement satisfies members' esteem needs (Maslow) and strengthens the cooperative's mutual loyalty, reducing the risk of the 5-day repair turnaround slipping further. Peer coaching also spreads tacit knowledge — stitching repairs, fabric matching, stain treatment — faster than external courses, builds confidence to tackle complex fabrics, and keeps hard-won skills inside LSP rather than concentrated in just 6 of 28 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to LSP's skills gap, cooperative structure and refurbishment workload.

questions.question_text: LSP must train 22 untrained staff in garment repair and refurbishment. Consider on-the-job mentoring by the 6 skilled repairers or off-the-job courses at a garment-repair college. Which should LSP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job mentoring: The 6 skilled repairers can coach colleagues directly at the workbench, teaching LSP's exact techniques — fabric matching, seam repair, hardware refitting — while trainees remain productive for the shop and online orders. It costs nothing in fees, suits the cooperative's peer-learning ethos, and fits the 5-day turnaround target. Its drawbacks are that the 6 mentors lose output while teaching, training quality depends on their teaching ability rather than a syllabus, and the most complex skills may take longer to master.

Off-the-job college courses: A structured college curriculum would give all 22 staff formal, certified instruction with external tutors and assessment, bringing in fresh techniques LSP does not currently use. However, fees across 22 staff would run into thousands of dollars against a $350,000 budget, generic content may not match LSP's pre-loved stock mix, and removing most of a 28-person team from the shop for course days would strain trading, the repair queue and the 5-day promise to parents.

Decision: LSP should choose on-the-job mentoring by the 6 skilled repairers. It is free, immediate, stock-specific and true to the cooperative's democratic, peer-led culture — decisive for a 28-person business launching a platform on a $350,000 budget. Off-the-job training is rejected as unaffordable at scale and too disruptive to current capacity; one or two mentors can later take a short college refresher themselves if complex-fabric skills plateau.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of on-the-job and off-the-job training with limited application to LSP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of LSP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of LSP with a well-justified decision covering cost, capacity and the cooperative ethos.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LSP's management can use its cost, break-even and average total cost data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($12.00 − $5.50) = $210,000 ÷ $6.50 = 32,307.69 units. Answer: break-even output is 32,307.69 units a year.
Formula: Average total cost = (Fixed costs ÷ Output) + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: ($210,000 ÷ 40,000 units) + $5.50 = $5.25 + $5.50 = $10.75. Answer: average total cost is $10.75 a unit.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LSP's management can use this break-even and average total cost data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. LSP's managers can compare the 32,307.69-unit break-even output with actual output of 40,000 units — a margin of safety of 7,692.31 units — to confirm the new e-commerce platform must beat a demanding volume target before launch is safe.
2. Average total cost of $10.75 against a $12.00 selling price yields $1.25 of clear profit per unit; managers can model a student-discount tier at $11.25 to test whether the volume gain offsets the thinner margin.
3. Break-even analysis tests the feasibility of the $220,000 bank loan at 5.5%: the platform must sell comfortably above 32,307.69 units a year to service repayments while still funding garment repair equipment and training.
4. Contribution per unit of $6.50 lets managers quantify the resale workshop's value: each refurbished garment (9,600 sold last year) contributes $6.50, guiding the sales mix between new and refurbished lines and informing decisions to expand repair capacity from the current 6 trained staff.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 32,307.69 units | (ii) Average total cost = $10.75 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 7,692.31 units against 40,000-unit output; price-tier modelling at $6.50 contribution; feasibility of the $220,000 bank loan at 5.5%; repair-capacity decisions for the 9,600 refurbished garments sold and the 6 trained staff.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LSP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LSP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.16 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.59 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $185,000. Current assets 2025 = $70,000 + $85,000 + $50,000 = $205,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $185,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.16; 2025 = $205,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.37. Stricter measure 2024 = ($185,000 − $90,000) ÷ $160,000 = $95,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.59; 2025 = ($205,000 − $70,000) ÷ $150,000 = $135,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.90.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved markedly. Short-term cover rose from 1.16 to 1.37 — comfortably above full cover — helped by current liabilities falling from $160,000 to $150,000 and current assets rising to $205,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.59 to 0.90, the strongest single-year gain, so LSP no longer depends on selling inventory to pay short-term debts — a vital milestone before launching the platform and taking on a $220,000 bank loan. Cautions: trade receivables climbed from $60,000 to $85,000 (platform sales on account) and should be collected promptly, and cash of $50,000 remains thin against a $350,000 project, leaving little room for cost overruns or slippage in launch revenue.

Conclusion: LSP's financial position has improved. Both measures strengthened (1.16 to 1.37 and 0.59 to 0.90), and the improvement does not rest on inventories, which actually fell from $90,000 to $70,000 as refurbished stock turned faster. LSP should collect receivables faster and phase platform spending carefully to protect cash during the launch so the stronger position endures.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether LSP's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LSP of launching a pre-loved childrenswear e-commerce platform.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The platform captures the 71% of surveyed parents who would buy pre-loved children's clothing online and the 18.5% market growth recorded last year, with the average parent saving $14 per garment versus new. It scales LSP's refurbishment workshop beyond its single Portland shop, leverages the 9,600 refurbished units already sold, attracts the 57% of buyers motivated by sustainability (core to LSP's cooperative mission) and builds a national customer base without the rent of additional stores.

Disadvantage: Success is capped by repair capacity — only 6 of 28 staff are trained, and turnaround already averages 5 days. If orders outrun the workshop, turnaround slips, parent complaints rise and the platform's reputation is damaged before it establishes. Fulfilment, photography and marketplace integration also add costs on top of the $350,000 investment, straining the $210,000 fixed-cost base if contribution per unit does not hold or if parents return items more often online.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LSP's research data, repair capacity and platform plan.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $13.60 and the 18.5% online resale market growth and 15.0% forecast expansion will affect LSP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (to 5.5%): LSP's $220,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, will cost roughly an extra $1,100 to $2,000 a year — small alongside fixed costs of $210,000. LSP can fix the rate and shield itself. Higher rates may slightly reduce consumers' willingness to borrow for discretionary purchases, though resale's saving positioning ($14 per garment versus new) is relatively resilient when household budgets are tight.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.60 per hour): For 28 mainly retail and workshop staff, the 6.0% rise is noticeable for a cooperative on modest margins. It strengthens the case for the repair upskilling programme because higher productivity per hour is the natural offset, and schedulers must be smarter about peak-hour cover to absorb it.

Online resale market growth (18.5% last year, forecast to expand a further 15.0% in 2027): This is a direct, measurable expansion of LSP's addressable market exactly as the platform launches. Capturing even a modest share of that growth would add thousands of orders, lift throughput beyond 40,000 units, fully utilise the repair workshop and push contribution well above current levels — dwarfing the interest-rate effect and offsetting the wage rise. The risk is failing to scale people and process fast enough to meet demand.

Conclusion: The 18.5% online resale market growth will have the greatest impact. It is strategic, not merely financial: it can determine whether the $350,000 platform creates step-change value or merely digitises a small shop. The wage rise is real and may be noticeable for the 28-person cooperative, but it is manageable through upskilling and peak-hour scheduling, and interest at 5.5% is minor and fixable. LSP should move quickly to train the 22 untrained members, lock supplier and freight deals and launch the platform while the window of 15.0% forecast growth is open — missing it forfeits the first-mover advantage in its home market.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to LSP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LSP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of LSP with a well-justified judgment that resale market growth has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
